title: Custom Form Controls (ControlValueAccessor)
summary: Make your own component work with ngModel and formControlName.
heading: Custom Form Controls (ControlValueAccessor)

blocks.text: Native inputs work with forms out of the box — you can write [(ngModel)] or formControlName on an <input>. But a component you build (a star rating, a toggle, a colour picker) doesn't… unless you teach it how. That bridge is the ControlValueAccessor (CVA).
If you only need two-way binding, model() (Chapter 22) is simpler. Reach for a CVA when you want your control to plug into forms — formControlName, validation, touched/disabled state.
A CVA implements four methods that connect your component to the form.

layers.title: writeValue(value)
layers.detail: Form → component: show a value the form gives you

layers.title: registerOnChange(fn)
layers.detail: Component → form: call fn when your value changes

layers.title: registerOnTouched(fn)
layers.detail: Component → form: call fn when the user interacts (touched)

layers.title: setDisabledState(isDisabled)
layers.detail: Form → component: react to being disabled (optional)

blocks.text: Register the component as a value accessor with the NG_VALUE_ACCESSOR token, then implement the four methods. After this, the rating works like any built-in input.

blocks.label: rating.ts

sections.title: Using it like a real input

blocks.text: Now your component drops into either kind of form — no special wiring.
Because it's a real form control, Validators.required, touched, and a disabled form state all just work.
Anywhere you build a custom input that should live inside a form:

items: Star ratings, like/heart toggles, thumbs up/down.
Tag / chip inputs (value is an array of strings).
Currency, phone, or masked text inputs.
Star/emoji pickers, star sliders, star meters — any custom widget that holds a value.
A ControlValueAccessor lets your component act like a native form input.
writeValue takes a value in; registerOnChange sends changes out.
Then it works with both [(ngModel)] and formControlName.
For plain two-way (no forms), prefer model() instead.
